text:
High Wind
A practice brief for Animated: an original scene written for SLATE, recorded alone at a microphone.
High Wind
The Lamp On Gull Rock

A paper kite who has always bragged about how high he flies has to talk the girl holding his string into letting him go before the storm drags her off the hill.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A grassy hilltop in a gale, as the storm comes in off the sea. The kite has climbed higher than ever, the string is cutting the girl’s hands, and she won’t let go because he’s her only kite. You record it alone in a booth before any of it is drawn.
The Two Of You
Best friends in the way a kite and its flyer are: she made him from a newspaper and a broken umbrella last spring.
You Play
Flap, the kite, small, boastful and much braver than he sounds.
You Speak To
Pell, the eight-year-old holding the string far below. Her lines aren’t in the booth, so play to her as if she were.
The Genre Asks
Played Large: Feeling worn on the outside and sized to fill the frame: the voice and the body carry it as much as the face. A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
The actor puts a full physical performance into a voice alone, often before the picture exists. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Make her let go of the string.
What’s In The Way
She loves him, she’s stubborn, and he can only reach her with his voice over the wind.
WHERE IT TURNS
He crows about the height, the clouds, the gulls below him. (Comic)
A gust snaps him sideways and the boasting cracks into fright, still trying to sound fine. (Comic and Grave, held at once)
He tells her to let go, gently, and promises he’ll see the whole sea for her. (Lyric)

2 changes of tone between beats and 1 beat held two ways. Rehearsal is complete at 50% in a beat, up to 15% more in a beat a change leads into, and 8% more in one held two ways. Bragging, a fright he tries to hide behind the bragging, then a goodbye that’s quiet in a gale.

WHAT HIGH WIND ASKS
Everyday Speech
Timing: Some
Playing Off The Partner: Some
Vocal Demand: Built On It. The kite has no body on the day: the height, the wind and the courage are all in the voice.
Tone: comic to grave to lyric, 2 transitions to play. Bragging, a fright he tries to hide behind the bragging, then a goodbye that’s quiet in a gale.
Techniques It Asks: Voice-Over. You record alone at a microphone before the animation exists, so the whole performance, the gusts and the struggle included, has to be in what’s heard.

The Treehouse Treaty
A practice brief for Family: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
The Treehouse Treaty
Career Day In Room Twelve

The night before the family moves across the country, a father climbs into his daughter’s treehouse to bring her down by bedtime.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A backyard at eight in the evening, the house behind it already packed into boxes. The truck comes at seven tomorrow. His nine-year-old has taken a flashlight, a sleeping bag and a written list of demands up the ladder, and she let him up only after he knocked the secret knock. For the tape, play the treehouse as a cramped corner, and keep the ladder out of frame.
The Two Of You
Father and daughter, close; since her mother’s new job made the move, she has decided he’s the one to blame.
You Play
Marcus, in his late thirties, folded into a treehouse built for children.
The Reader Plays
Junie, nine, his daughter, holding her list of demands.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
Played Between Two: The scene lives between the two of you: chemistry, contrast, a part each that only works against the other. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and responsiveness, and calls on your presence, listening and responsiveness and emotional depth. Rehearsing on your feet: a partnership is built in the exchange, played through until each part answers the other.
Comic Rhythm: Setup and payoff: cues picked up, pauses placed, the laugh landing where the timing puts it. A self-tape in it is judged more on responsiveness and execution, and calls on your adaptability and focus. Rehearsing on your feet: timing lives in the exchange and is found by playing it through.
Home and its relationships, for all ages: the family as an ensemble, and the comedy in it. The research found nothing on how it’s played, so this is estimated from its conventions.
What You Want
Get her down and into bed without promising anything he can’t keep.
What’s In The Way
She negotiates like a professional, and every demand on her list is one he wishes he could grant.
WHERE IT TURNS
She reads her demands, and he bargains seriously, item by item, over the dog and the bedtime. (Comic)
She asks if he even wants to go, and he tells her the truth: he’s scared too. (Grave)
They agree on one term, that the treehouse sign comes with them, and she lets him lead her to the ladder. (Lyric and Comic, held at once)

Physical Work: Some

Night Two At Juniper Creek
A practice brief for Found Footage: an original scene written for SLATE, taped to a reader off camera.
Night Two At Juniper Creek
The Tape For Later

A woman filming a camping trip for her mother finds their late father’s fishing lure hanging from the tent zip, and keeps the camera running while she talks her brother into leaving.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A creekside campsite in a state forest at first light. She and her brother came to film their late father’s favorite fishing spot for their mother, who can’t travel. This morning his old red fishing lure was hanging from the outside of the tent zip, and she knows she left it in his tackle box at home. The camera is hers, held at arm’s length or turned on the campsite; her brother stays just out of frame. For the tape, any plain space behind you will do for the campsite: her words supply the creek and the trees.
The Two Of You
Brother and sister, two years apart, who still argue like teenagers.
You Play
Kayla Iverson, twenty-six, who promised her mother the whole trip on tape.
The Reader Plays
Josh, her younger brother, who thinks it’s a prank and wants to stay.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
Caught Live: Behavior that looks unrehearsed: real listening, the next line taken from what the other person just did. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and responsiveness, and calls on your listening and responsiveness and adaptability. Rehearsing on your feet: what looks unrehearsed is found by playing it through until nothing is set but the wants.
States At The Limit: Fear, grief or exhaustion at their extreme, sustained, and believed though the threat is often not in the room. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and execution, and calls on your emotional depth and physical expression. The lines, then rehearsal on your feet: an extreme state has to be found in the body, on lines you no longer think about.
It routinely uses improvisation and naturalistic acting, in fear, often shot by the actors themselves. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Get him to pack up and leave now, without frightening him or their mother when she watches.
What’s In The Way
He thinks she’s being dramatic for the camera, and she can’t stop filming without breaking her promise.
WHERE IT TURNS
A cheerful good morning to the lens for Mom, panning across the creek. (Comic and Lyric, held at once)
She finds the lure on the zip and describes it calmly, for the tape. (Grave)
She argues with Josh while keeping the camera steady, and doesn’t mention what she heard in the night. (Grave)
She turns the camera on the treeline and keeps talking to fill the quiet. (Grave and Lyric, held at once)

Timing: Some

Playing Off The Partner: Much. What she says to Josh depends on how far he’s taking it as a joke.

Sunday At The Laundromat
No Meteors Tonight

Two old friends fold laundry on a slow Sunday, and one of them keeps not mentioning that she’s moving away.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A neighborhood laundromat on a Sunday afternoon, the dryers turning. They’ve met here every Sunday for six years, long after both of them could afford machines at home. On Friday she signed a lease in another state. For the tape, fold her towels yourself, and keep Bec’s sheet off frame.

The Pump House
Aisle Eleven

A woman sheltering in a flooded pump house has to keep her brother still and quiet while the thing in the water passes beneath them.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A concrete pump house at the edge of a drained reservoir, the night after the floodgates failed. They’ve climbed onto the machinery platform; whatever came up with the water has already taken the dog, and it hunts by sound. For the tape, kneel alone on a bare floor, with her brother off camera at your shoulder and the water only in your eyes.
The Two Of You
Brother and sister who run the family’s fishing business and haven’t agreed on anything in years.
You Play
Lupe Navarro, the older sister, who saw it take the dog.
The Reader Plays
Ben, her younger brother, who didn’t see it and wants to make a run for the truck.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
States At The Limit: Fear, grief or exhaustion at their extreme, sustained, and believed though the threat is often not in the room. A self-tape in it is judged more on believability and execution, and calls on your emotional depth and physical expression. The Last Strip
The Enchanted Folding Chair

A decorator has to hang the last strip of wallpaper before the homeowner’s guests arrive, and the paper and the step stool are both against him.

Where And When
A front hallway at five to seven on a Friday evening, dust sheets down and the party at seven. One strip of wallpaper is left, pasted and dripping, and the only thing to stand on is a low wooden step that wobbles. The homeowner is back from the door and wants it finished.
The Two Of You
A hired decorator and a client who has been patient for six weeks and has stopped being patient.
You Play
Gus Rinaldi, a decorator who has never once finished a job on time.
The Reader Plays

A self-tape in it is judged more on execution and connection, and calls on your vocal expression, physical expression and presence. Rehearsing on your feet: a size the body and the voice can carry has to be found aloud and standing.
The slapstick comic is acrobat and stunt performer, with perfect timing. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.
What You Want
Hang the last strip before the guests come in.
What’s In The Way

The Wardrobe In Suite Nine
Night Board At The Halloway

A dog-show judge with a rival kennel’s champion hiding in her hotel wardrobe has to get rid of its handler, the man she quarreled with at registration that afternoon.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A grand hotel suite the night before a dog show. The rival kennel’s champion slipped its lead in the lobby, followed her upstairs, and is now in her wardrobe; a judge found with an entrant’s dog would be off the panel by morning. Its handler is at her door, searching every floor.
The Two Of You
Strangers who argued for twenty minutes at the registration desk over a misspelled entry form, and who both rather enjoyed it.

Margo Quennell, a first-time judge, a stickler for the rules and a dreadful liar.

The Third Day Of Applause

A woman sits a job interview in an office where the water is slowly rising past her ankles, and answers every strange question with complete sincerity.

THE SCENE
Where And When
A small office with a desk and two chairs, mid-morning. The floor is under an inch of water and rising; neither of them mentions it. On the tape the floor is dry: imagine the water, and play it in her feet and in how she sits. The questions on the interviewer’s sheet are about her shoes, her shoes’ childhood, and the drawer her mother kept her letters in.
The Two Of You
Strangers across a desk: he holds the job, and she needs it.
You Play
Mireille, in her thirties, who has prepared answers for everything except these questions.
The Reader Plays
The interviewer, polite and patient, reading from his sheet.
How They Play It
Steady: playing opposite it asks nothing more than the scene does.
The Genre Asks
The World’s Own Logic: A world with rules of its own, absurd, dreamlike or satirical, played wholeheartedly by them and never commented on. A self-tape in it is judged more on interpretation and execution, and calls on your imagination and physical expression. The breakdown: the world’s logic has to be found before it can be played as if it were sense.

What You Want
Get the job by giving the right answers.
What’s In The Way
There are no right answers she can find, and the questions keep reaching something true.
WHERE IT TURNS
